cells.tense: Fairness is moving easily between you and the ones you feel with, and the pen is in your hand.
cells.act: let the old form go so the next one can come
cells.ask: Let an arrangement between you and someone close end — one you both kept going well past the point it fit. Close it. Don't reopen it. Then see what the two of you have room for with the old form gone.
cells.core:
You feel what's off between you and the people close to you before it's spoken. Give and take move without a score kept, and your sense of what's fair arrives without arithmetic. The hard part is knowing when something between you has finished. You'd rather hold the shape you have than let it be over.

Let one arrangement end that served when you set it up and doesn't now. Some of the comfort goes with it — the form was doing quiet work, and putting it down leaves a gap. That's the cost. But ending it is the fair move, and the ones inside it already feel the pull. Nothing new arrives while the old thing stands in its place.
cells.sheetLine: Fair to them a year ago isn't fair to them now.
cells.verb: calling what's out of proportion back to true
cells.place: beside the ones you feel with

cells.tense: What you feel between people is turning into arithmetic — everything owed will be settled before the hour is out.
cells.act: carry it without tightening around it
cells.ask: Next time something feels off between you and someone, carry it an hour without settling anything — no score, no fix, no case built. Put the tally down. The fact stays; the arithmetic doesn't.
cells.core:
You track what people owe and what's owed to you faster than you'd admit, and the tracking has begun to be the relationship itself. Nothing is quite settled, so everything gets weighed ahead of time. Underneath, the wish is fair: you want things right between you and you want them right now.

Name the imbalance once, to the person or in your own head, then carry it an hour and decide nothing. Put the score down. The fact stays, the arithmetic doesn't, and the weight you were braced for turns out to be mostly the bracing. When fairness has room to move again, give and take flow without anyone keeping a tally on either side.
cells.sheetLine: You're tallying what nobody asked you to settle.
cells.verb: calling what's out of proportion back to true
cells.place: beside the ones you feel with

cells.tense: Where you feel with people, something owed went unclaimed, and the moment for it has already closed.
cells.act: keep the steady light lit by attention, not flash
cells.ask: Go back to the small practice you keep meaning to return to. Ten minutes, alone, today, before it's planned. Keep it for its own sake, not as a fix and not about anyone else.
cells.core:
You feel what's off with people, and you don't move to claim what's yours inside it. Fairness has come to feel like it costs too much, so the tab goes unpaid and the room stays as it is. What's gone quiet is the part of you that knows what's due to you.

Go back to a small practice you do alone: a thing you keep meaning to return to, ten minutes, today. Do it before you've planned it. Keeping one steady thing for its own sake recharges the part that's quiet now. Doing it for yourself, not against anyone, is what makes fairness feel safe enough to lift again. It comes back up through the floor, not on demand. Nobody needs to watch, and nobody needs to be told.
cells.sheetLine: You can feel the imbalance and you don't go get what's owed.

cells.tense: The tally is running between you and the ones you feel with, and you'd say you haven't been counting.
cells.act: write the first thing you knew about it, before the reasons
cells.ask: About something unsettled between you and someone, write down the first thing you knew before the reasons came. Set it down and add nothing. Read it back later if you want.
cells.core:
You feel with the ones close to you and keep the room fair, then tell it as though you had nothing to do with it. What you've actually done is weigh things: small scores you didn't sit down to keep, unfairnesses you noticed and didn't name. The fair call has been made in you. The account of it doesn't include you making it.

Go back to the simpler thing that comes before the weighing: what you knew about a situation between people the moment you knew it, ahead of any argument. Put it in a line on paper, once, and add nothing to it. The true thing often arrives quietly before reasons. The question is whether you'll count that first knowing as something you did.
cells.sheetLine: You weigh what's fair between people and say you don't.
cells.verb: calling what's out of proportion back to true
